records.content_text:
In Chapter 4, you learnt that a common fraction is written as two whole numbers, one on top of the other: $\frac{\text{numerator}}{\text{denominator}}$.

- The denominator represents all the parts of a whole. For example, in the fraction $\frac{2}{7}$, each whole is divided into 7 parts.
- The numerator represents only the parts of a whole we are dealing with. For example, in the fraction $\frac{2}{7}$, we are dealing with only 2 out of 7 parts.

Usman and Adamu are at a birthday party. There is a cake that is cut into 4 pieces:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-001.png)

Suppose Usman gets $\frac{1}{4}$ of the cake:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-035.png)

Suppose Adamu also gets $\frac{1}{4}$ of the cake:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-002.png)

If they put their pieces of cake together, they have $\frac{2}{4}$ of the cake:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-003.png)

We write this as:

$$
\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{2}{4}
$$

In Chapter 4, you learnt how to write a fraction in its simplest form. This is when the numerator and denominator have no common factor.

The simplest form of $\frac{2}{4}$ is $\frac{1}{2}$.

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-004.png)

records.content_text:
Suppose another cake arrives at the birthday party that Usman and Adamu are attending. This cake is also cut into 4 pieces. Someone immediately takes a piece, so that only 3 of the 4 pieces are left. The cake may now be represented as follows.

There is $\frac{3}{4}$ of the cake left:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-036.png)

Danladi did not have any cake yet. He gets 1 piece, which is $\frac{1}{4}$ of the cake:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-005.png)

After Danladi took his piece, $\frac{2}{4}$ of the cake is left:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-037.png)

We write this as:

$$
\frac{3}{4}-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{2}{4}
$$
The simplest form of $\frac{2}{4}$ is $\frac{1}{2}$.

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-06-006.png)

We may therefore write:

$$
\frac{3}{4}-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

heading_path.h3: Worked example 6.2: Subtracting fractions with the same denominator

placement.rationale: This worked example subtracts fractions with the same denominator.

records.evidence_quote: Calculate: $$ \frac{7}{9}-\frac{3}{9} $$
records.prompt_text:
Calculate:

$$
\frac{7}{9}-\frac{3}{9}
$$
records.answer_text:
Method 1: Using diagrams

1. The denominator shows into how many parts one whole must be divided. Represent this in a diagram. In this case, there must be 9 parts.

2. Shade the number of parts shown by the first numerator. The first numerator is 7.

3. Scratch out the number of parts shown by the numerator that is subtracted. The second numerator is 3. We must scratch out 3 parts.

4. Redraw the diagram, shading only the parts that are left over. There are 4 parts left over.

5. Write the shaded part as a fraction.

$$
\frac{4}{9}
$$

6. Check whether the fraction is in its simplest form.

In this case, the numerator and denominator have no common factors.

7. The full calculation is:

$$
\begin{array}{l}
 \phantom{00}\frac{7}{9}-\frac{3}{9}\newline
 =\frac{4}{9} \newline
 \end{array}
$$

Method 2: Calculating directly

1. The denominator shows into how many parts one whole must be divided. Write down the denominator.

$$
\begin{array}{l}
 \phantom{00}\frac{7}{9}-\frac{3}{9}\newline
 =\frac{\phantom{0000}}{9} \newline
 \end{array}
$$

2. Write down the numerators that must be subtracted.

$$
\begin{array}{l}
 \phantom{00}\frac{7}{9}-\frac{3}{9}\newline
 =\frac{7-3}{9} \newline
 \end{array}
$$

3. Subtract the numerators.

$$
\begin{array}{l}
 \phantom{00}\frac{7}{9}-\frac{3}{9}\newline
 =\frac{7-3}{9} \newline
 =\frac{4}{9} \newline
 \end{array}
$$

4. Simplify the answer if necessary. In this case, is it not necessary.

records.content_text:
Suppose we want to determine the following:

$$
\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{2}
$$

$$
\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}
$$

\frac{2}{3} of a cake may be represented as:

\frac{1}{2} of a cake may be represented as:

We can divide one cake into either 2 pieces or 3 pieces. We cannot divide the cake into both. To overcome this problem, we have to express both fractions with the same denominator. The lowest common denominator (LCD) of 2 and 3 is 6. The equivalent fractions of \frac{2}{3} and \frac{1}{2}, with 6 as their denominator, are:

$$
\frac{2}{3}=\frac{2\times2}{3\times2}=\frac{4}{6}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1\times3}{2\times3}=\frac{3}{6}
$$

Now we can follow the same method as before.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 6.3: Adding fractions with different denominators

placement.rationale: This worked example adds fractions with different denominators by first finding the LCD.

records.evidence_quote: Calculate: $$ \frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{2} $$
records.prompt_text:
Calculate:

$$
\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{2}
$$
records.answer_text:
Step 1: Compare the denominators. If they are different, find the LCD.

The LCD of 2 and 3 is 6.

Step 2: Find equivalent fractions with the LCD as their denominators.

$$
\frac{2}{3}=\frac{4}{6}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{6}
$$

Step 3: Use the LCD to represent the parts of one whole in a diagram.

In this case, there must be 6 parts.

Step 4: Shade the number of parts shown by the first numerator of the equivalent fraction.

This is 4.

Step 5: Shade the additional parts shown by the second numerator of the equivalent fraction.

The second numerator is 3. We must shade another 3 parts.

There are only 2 "gaps" in the shape that can be shaded. Therefore, we need to add another shape.

Step 6: Write the total shaded part as a fraction.

The fraction is \frac{7}{6}.

Remember, the denominator shows into how many parts one whole is divided. The numerator shows the total number of those parts that we are dealing with.

Step 7: Write the answer in its simplest form or as a mixed number.

$$
\frac{7}{6}=1\frac{1}{6}
$$

Step 8: Write out the whole calculation.

$$
\begin{array}{l}
 \phantom{00}\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{2}\newline
 =\frac{4}{6}+\frac{3}{6}\newline
 =\frac{4+3}{6} \newline
 =\frac{7}{6} \newline
 =1\frac{1}{6}
 \end{array}
$$

$$
records.answer_text:
Step 1: Compare the denominators. If they are different, find the LCD.

The LCD of 2 and 3 is 6.

Step 2: Find equivalent fractions with the LCD as their denominators.

$$
\frac{2}{3}=\frac{4}{6}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{6}
$$

Step 3: Use the LCD to represent the parts of one whole in a diagram.

In this case, there must be 6 parts.

Step 4: Shade the number of parts shown by the first numerator of the equivalent fraction.

This is 4.

Step 5: Scratch out the number of parts shown by the numerator of the equivalent fraction that is subtracted. Then redraw the diagram with only the parts that are left over shaded.

The second numerator is 3. We must scratch out 3 parts.

There is only one part left over.

Step 6: Write the shaded part as a fraction.

$$
\frac{1}{6}
$$

Step 7: Check whether the fraction is in its simplest form.

In this case, the numerator and denominator have no common factors.

Step 8: Write out the whole calculation.

$$
\begin{array}{l}

 =\frac{4}{6}-\frac{3}{6}\newline

heading_path.h3: Worked example 6.5: Adding mixed numbers

placement.rationale: This worked example adds mixed numbers by converting them to improper fractions.

records.evidence_quote: Calculate: $$ 2\frac{4}{5}+1\frac{2}{3} $$
records.prompt_text:
Calculate:

$$
2\frac{4}{5}+1\frac{2}{3}
$$
records.answer_text:
Step 1: Convert the mixed numbers to improper fractions.

$$
2\frac{4}{5}=\frac{(2\times5)+4}{5}=\frac{14}{5}
$$

$$
1\frac{2}{3}=\frac{(1\times3)+2}{3}=\frac{5}{3}
$$

Step 2: If the denominators differ, find equivalent fractions with the LCD as their denominators.

The LCD of 3 and 5 is 15.

$$
\frac{14}{5}=\frac{42}{15}
$$

$$
\frac{5}{3}=\frac{25}{15}
$$

Step 3: Write down the LCD and add the numerators of the equivalent fractions.

$$
\begin{array}{l}
 \phantom{00}\frac{42}{15}+\frac{25}{15}\\
 =\frac{42+25}{15} \\
 =\frac{67}{15}
 \end{array}
$$

Step 4: Simplify the answer by converting the improper fraction to a mixed number.

$$
\begin{array}{l}
 \phantom{00}\frac{42}{15}+\frac{25}{15}\\
 =\frac{42+25}{15} \\
 =\frac{67}{15} \\
 =4\frac{7}{15} \\
 \end{array}
$$

records.evidence_quote: - To add or subtract fractions with the same denominator: - Write down the denominator. - Then add or subtract the numerators. - To add or subtract fractions with different denominators: - Find the LCD. - Find equivalent fractions with the LCD as denominator. - Then add or subtract the numerators. - To multiply fractio
records.content_text:
- To add or subtract fractions with the same denominator:
  - Write down the denominator.
  - Then add or subtract the numerators.
- To add or subtract fractions with different denominators:
  - Find the LCD.
  - Find equivalent fractions with the LCD as denominator.
  - Then add or subtract the numerators.
- To multiply fractions and whole numbers:
  - Write down the denominator of the fraction.
  - Multiply the numerator of the fraction by the whole number.
- To multiply fractions with fractions:
  - Multiply the numerators.
  - Multiply the denominators.
- The reciprocal of a fraction is the "opposite" of the fraction, which we get by swapping the numerator and denominator. Whole numbers also have reciprocals. For example:
  - The reciprocal of $\frac{4}{9}$ is $\frac{9}{4}$.
  - The reciprocal of 8 is $\frac{1}{8}$.
- Dividing by a fraction or whole number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal. For example:
  - $$\frac{4}{9}\div 8=\frac{4}{9}\times\frac{1}{8}$$
  - $$\frac{4}{9}\div \frac{3}{5}=\frac{4}{9}\times\frac{5}{3}$$
- Before you add, subtract, multiply or divide mixed numbers, first convert them to improper fractions.
- When you have to multiply fractions with large numerators or denominators, simplify first.
